articles.title: In 2009, a California pier walk began raising money for children with special needs; 17 years later, supporters including Sugar Ray Leonard and Brooke Burke helped it record a $3.3 million fundraising year
articles.summary: A community walk that began as an effort to support children with special needs has grown into one of Southern California's major annual charity events,
articles.body: A community walk that began as an effort to support children with special needs has grown into one of Southern California's major annual charity events, bringing together thousands of participants, celebrities and corporate sponsors. What started as a local fundraising initiative has now raised millions of dollars for children, students and young adults, helping fund educational opportunities, inclusive programmes and facilities designed to support independence.According to an October 23, 2026, announcement by the National Sporting Goods Association (NSGA), the 18th annual Skechers Pier to Pier Friendship Walk raised a record $3.3 million. Organised by the Skechers Foundation and the Friendship Foundation, with Nickelodeon as presenting sponsor, the event attracted more than 24,000 registrants. Among its supporters were boxing legend Sugar Ray Leonard, television host Brooke Burke, actor Nate Simon and baseball players Chris Taylor, Kyle Karros and Jared Karros.How a community walk became a major charity eventThe Skechers Pier to Pier Friendship Walk brings together families, students, volunteers, celebrities and businesses for a 3.4-mile journey along Southern California's South Bay coastline. The annual event supports children with special needs, public school education and college scholarships. Over its 18-year history, the initiative has raised $35 million, according to Skechers president and walk co-founder Michael Greenberg. He said participants had collectively walked more than one million miles, equivalent to travelling around the planet approximately 40 times.The event has developed beyond a fundraising walk into a platform for raising awareness about inclusion and providing practical support to children and young adults. Its proceeds help finance programmes that address educational needs, improve school facilities and create opportunities for individuals with developmental and learning differences. The 2026 edition was particularly significant because it recorded the event's highest-ever fundraising total, with $3.3 million collected in support of its beneficiaries.A $70 million campus for neurodivergent young adultsOne of the major projects supported by the annual walk is the Friendship Campus, also known as The Greenberg Family/Skechers Center. The $70 million development covers nearly 62,000 square feet and is designed to provide neurodivergent young adults with a supportive environment where they can develop independence, discover their interests and prepare for adult life.Funded by the Skechers Foundation, the Friendship Foundation and other partners, the campus is scheduled to open on January 21, 2027. Its facilities will include a creative arts studio, a culinary institute and a recreation centre. It will also offer life-skills programmes, early education and mentoring opportunities to help participants build confidence and prepare for meaningful professional opportunities. The campus will become the new headquarters of the Friendship Foundation, allowing the organisation to expand its programmes and reach more families across Los Angeles County.The foundation's work has grown considerably since its beginnings. Its original buddy programme served just 30 participants at one school. It now engages more than 5,000 students, participants and volunteers across the county, working with nearly 100 schools. Its activities include more than 50 monthly programmes and a six-week summer camp for children with special needs.How the walk supports schools and studentsBeyond its work with children with special needs, the Skechers Pier to Pier Friendship Walk also directs funding towards public education. Through partnerships with public school education foundations, the event has contributed millions of dollars to improve learning environments. The money has helped reduce class sizes, upgrade science laboratories and libraries, improve school facilities and protect teaching jobs.Another part of the proceeds supports the Skechers Foundation's national college scholarship programme. The initiative has awarded more than $3.5 million in scholarships to students who demonstrate financial need alongside achievement in academics, athletics and leadership. These contributions allow the event to support students at different stages of their education, from school improvements to financial assistance for higher studies.Celebrities and businesses join the causeThe 2026 walk attracted several well-known supporters, including Sugar Ray Leonard, Brooke Burke and actor Nate Simon. Baseball players Chris Taylor, Kyle Karros and Jared Karros also joined the initiative.Participants were entertained by performances from the Full Circle Boys and the Los Angeles Clippers Spirit dance team. Popular Nickelodeon characters, including SpongeBob, Sandy, the Paw Patrol characters Marshall and Everest, and Rugrats characters Tommy and Angelica, also interacted with attendees. The event included an animal adoption activity organised in partnership with Best Friends Animal Society, giving shelter animals an opportunity to find new homes.Nickelodeon served as the presenting sponsor, while several companies and organisations contributed to the event, including Rare Beauty, Mattel, Big 5 Sporting Goods, Bank of America, Amazon, KPMG, Honda and the Los Angeles Dodgers.A growing commitment to inclusionThe record $3.3 million raised in 2026 reflects the scale of support the annual walk has built over nearly two decades. Its impact extends beyond a single fundraising day, helping finance educational improvements, scholarships and programmes that give children and young adults greater opportunities.With the Friendship Campus preparing to open in January 2027, the initiative is also moving towards a new phase of support for neurodivergent young adults. Its organisers hope to create more opportunities for participants to develop practical skills, build relationships and pursue meaningful futures.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: A North Dakota mother withheld the children from their father and stopped communication, a court found; the state Supreme Court upheld a contempt ruling awarding him 19 weekends of make-up parenting time
articles.summary: Parenting schedules are meant to ensure that children maintain relationships with both parents, but disputes can arise when one parent repeatedly prevents
articles.body: Parenting schedules are meant to ensure that children maintain relationships with both parents, but disputes can arise when one parent repeatedly prevents the other from exercising court-ordered parenting time. In North Dakota, a mother's decision to withhold her children from their father and stop communicating with him led to a contempt finding and an order granting the father 19 weekends of make-up parenting time.In a November 6, 2026, decision available on Justia, the North Dakota Supreme Court upheld the contempt ruling against Christa Sandstrom in a dispute involving Courtney Krueger. The court found no clear error in the lower court's conclusion that Sandstrom had willfully and inexcusably withheld the children from their father. It also upheld the remedial sanction of additional parenting time, rejecting her argument that the 19 weekends were punitive rather than intended to address the missed visits.How the parenting dispute developedThe case, Krueger v. Sandstrom, involved disagreements over parenting arrangements and allegations that Sandstrom had prevented Krueger from spending time with their children. Krueger sought enforcement of the existing parenting arrangement after the mother allegedly withheld the children and stopped communicating with him. The dispute eventually led to an evidentiary hearing in the district court. Sandstrom also sought to modify the existing parenting-time arrangement, arguing that circumstances had changed and that the court should reconsider the children's schedule.During the hearing, she wanted two witnesses to testify about an ongoing criminal investigation. The court declined to require their testimony on that subject but gave her two options: withdraw her motion and refile it later, or continue with the hearing without those witnesses. Sandstrom chose to proceed. The district court subsequently denied her request to modify parenting time, found her in contempt and awarded Krueger 19 weekends of make-up parenting time as a remedial sanction. It also awarded him attorney's fees.Why the mother challenged the rulingSandstrom appealed several parts of the district court's decision. She argued that the court should have granted her a continuance after restricting the proposed testimony about the active criminal investigation. She also maintained that the district court's findings were insufficient and that it had improperly limited her ability to present evidence of a material change in circumstances. According to her argument, the excluded testimony was relevant to her request to modify the existing parenting arrangement.Under North Dakota law, a parent seeking to modify parenting time must demonstrate that a material change in circumstances has occurred since the previous order and that the proposed modification would serve the children's best interests. The state Supreme Court noted that a material change generally involves important new facts that were unknown when the original parenting-time order was entered.The district court had considered the abuse allegations and the factors relevant to the children's best interests. It found that no material change in circumstances had been established. The Supreme Court concluded that these findings were sufficient and were not clearly erroneous.Why the Supreme Court upheld the 19 weekendsA central issue in the appeal was whether the district court had properly found Sandstrom in contempt and whether awarding Krueger 19 weekends of additional parenting time was an appropriate remedy. Sandstrom argued that the sanction was punitive in effect rather than remedial. She challenged the court's authority to impose such an arrangement as a response to the missed parenting time.The Supreme Court explained that determining whether contempt has occurred and whether remedial sanctions are justified falls within the district court's discretion. An appellate court will not overturn such a decision unless there has been a clear abuse of that discretion.In this case, the district court specifically found that Sandstrom had willfully and inexcusably withheld the children from Krueger and stopped communicating with him. The Supreme Court found no clear error in those findings. It also concluded that the district court had not abused its discretion by awarding 19 weekends of make-up parenting time.The additional weekends were treated as a remedial measure intended to address the parenting time Krueger had lost because of the mother's conduct. The court therefore upheld both the contempt finding and the additional parenting-time award.What happened to the attorney's feesSandstrom also challenged the attorney's fees awarded to Krueger. She questioned whether the district court had authority to determine the amount after an appeal had already been filed and argued that the award was not adequately supported. The Supreme Court explained that under North Dakota Rule of Civil Procedure 54(e)(2), a court can decide a timely attorney's fees motion even after an appeal has been filed. Krueger had submitted his request in time, so the district court had authority to determine the fees.However, the Supreme Court declined to review Sandstrom's separate challenge to the amount awarded. Her notice of appeal had been filed before the district court issued the order setting the amount, and she had not amended the notice or filed another appeal after that order. As a result, the issue was not properly preserved for appellate review.What the ruling meansIn its November 6, 2026, decision, the North Dakota Supreme Court summarily affirmed the district court's orders denying Sandstrom's request to modify parenting time, finding her in contempt, denying her continuance and awarding remedial sanctions and attorney's fees. The ruling reinforces that parents must comply with existing parenting-time orders unless they are formally changed by a court. It also shows that make-up parenting time can serve as a remedial sanction when one parent has deliberately prevented the other from exercising court-ordered visits.The decision does not establish a new parenting schedule or resolve the underlying family dispute in its entirety. Instead, it upholds the lower court's findings and the 19 additional weekends awarded to Krueger.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.summary: LUCKNOW: Chief minister Yogi Adityanath on Wednesday defended the bursting of firecrackers during Diwali, saying he had personally participated in
articles.body: LUCKNOW: Chief minister Yogi Adityanath on Wednesday defended the bursting of firecrackers during Diwali, saying he had personally participated in celebrations in Ayodhya and arguing that concerns over pollution were being selectively raised.Speaking at an event in Lucknow, Yogi said people were now able to celebrate Diwali and other festivals "without fear" and criticised those who, he claimed, objected to firecrackers.Referring to complaints about air quality, he said pollution may increase during Diwali but would also subside. "Lots of people said there was pollution due to Diwali celebrations. I said pollution did happen but it will end also. Why worry about it?" he said. The chief minister used the remarks to target political opponents, alleging that while corruption had "polluted the entire system," criticism was directed at common people celebrating for a single day. He maintained that any pollution caused by crackers was temporary and not a major issue, adding that it was good people celebrated Diwali with "dhoom dharaka." He said he was happy that large numbers of people lit firecrackers.Yogi reiterated his govt's stance of imposing no restrictions on Diwali celebrations and said he was in Ayodhya during the lighting of firecrackers. He also said that festivals had been celebrated with grandeur this year. Contrasting the present with the period before 2017, the chief minister claimed festivals were earlier preceded by riots and curfews, which affected markets and public safety. He said that over the past 9.5 years there had been no curfews and no "danga," adding that the situation in Uttar Pradesh had changed.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Two Ohio co-owners fought over proceeds from a property sale, with one receiving $171,635 and the other $23,161; on November 9, an appeals court dismissed the smaller recipient's challenge after both were paid
articles.summary: An Ohio appeals court has dismissed a man's challenge to the division of money from a property sale after the funds were released to him and his former
articles.body: An Ohio appeals court has dismissed a man's challenge to the division of money from a property sale after the funds were released to him and his former co-owner. The man, Randall W. Petersen, had argued that he received less than his rightful share of the proceeds. However, the court said he could no longer pursue the appeal because the lower court's order had already been carried out.The Eleventh District Court of Appeals of Ohio delivered its decision on November 9. It dismissed Petersen's appeal against a February 2026 judgment that awarded him $23,161.36 from the property sale. The other co-owner, Andrea M Mackey, was awarded $171,635.According to the ruling, the dispute concerned the division of proceeds from the sale of a property in Concord Township, Ohio. The two co-owners had earlier agreed on how the money would be divided. However, they could not reach a final agreement on the distribution, leaving the trial court to decide how much each person should receive.Petersen challenged the lower court's calculation, arguing that it had not properly accounted for his financial contributions to the property. But before examining whether his claim had merit, the appeals court considered whether it could hear the case at all. It found that the money had already been distributed and Petersen had not obtained an order stopping the payment while his appeal was pending.How the dispute over the property sale beganThe legal dispute started in November 2023, when Mackey filed a partition lawsuit against Petersen in the Lake County Court of Common Pleas. The case concerned a property in Concord Township. She also named the Lake County Treasurer and Third Federal Savings and Loan Association of Cleveland as defendants.A partition action is a legal process used to resolve disputes involving jointly owned property. It can lead to the division or sale of the property when co-owners cannot agree on what should happen to it.In February 2024, Petersen responded to the lawsuit. He also filed a counterclaim alleging conversion of personal property. He claimed that Mackey had taken certain belongings while she had sole possession of the property.The parties later reached a settlement concerning the property and its pending sale. In May 2025, the trial court recorded their agreement through an agreed judgment entry and dismissal.One of the important terms dealt with the money expected from the sale. Both parties agreed that the proceeds would remain in an escrow account held by the title company until they decided how to divide the amount.They also agreed on the principles for distributing the money between them. However, the agreement provided another option if they failed to reach a mutual decision. In that situation, the court would arrange a hearing, hear testimony and consider the evidence before deciding how the proceeds should be divided.The court also retained the authority to enforce the settlement terms. This meant it could intervene if the parties disagreed over how the agreement should be implemented.Court awards Mackey $171,635 and Petersen $23,161The disagreement over the distribution eventually led to a hearing on January 16, 2026. Since the parties could not settle the matter themselves, the trial court considered the issue and decided how much each co-owner should receive.Several weeks later, the court issued its judgment. It awarded Mackey $171,635 from the sale proceeds and Petersen $23,161.36.The court directed the escrow company to release the respective amounts to the two parties and close the account. The order settled the question of how the money held from the property sale would be distributed.Petersen subsequently challenged the decision before the Eleventh District Court of Appeals. His appeal focused on the amount awarded to him.He argued that the trial court had incorrectly calculated his share of the property's net sale proceeds. According to his appeal, the court should have given him credit for mortgage payments and other qualifying contributions that he had made towards increasing the property's equity.In other words, Petersen believed that his financial contributions had not been properly considered when the lower court calculated his entitlement. He sought a review of the amount awarded to him.Appeals court says completed payment makes challenge mootHowever, the appeals court first had to consider an objection raised by Mackey. She argued that Petersen's appeal had become moot because the escrow funds had already been released to both parties in accordance with the trial court's order.The appeals court agreed with her argument. It explained that when a court's judgment has been voluntarily paid and satisfied, an appeal against that judgment generally becomes moot.The court relied on an earlier Ohio Supreme Court decision, Blodgett v. Blodgett, which established that satisfaction of a judgment can bring an end to the dispute and remove the right to appeal.The principle applies when a court has jurisdiction over the case and the parties, and there has been no fraud. Once a judgment is voluntarily paid and satisfied, the losing party generally cannot continue challenging it through an appeal.The judges also pointed out that Petersen had not filed a motion seeking a stay of the trial court's judgment while his appeal was pending.A stay is an order that temporarily stops the enforcement of a court's decision. In this case, obtaining a stay could have prevented the escrow company from distributing the money until the appeal was decided.The appeals court said that failing to obtain such an order meant the distribution could go ahead. Since the funds had been released, the lower court's judgment had been satisfied.It referred to its earlier decision in Edwards v. Wilcox (2024), which also dealt with an appeal in a property partition dispute. In that case, the court had held that an appeal becomes moot when the judgment has been satisfied and the appellant has failed to obtain a stay.The judges also cited other Ohio court decisions supporting the same legal principle. These included cases involving settlement proceeds distributed without a stay and funds released from escrow under a trial court's order.Court finds no reason to make an exceptionThe appeals court also considered whether the case could fall under either of the recognised exceptions to the mootness doctrine.These exceptions apply to matters that are capable of repetition but likely to avoid review, or cases involving an issue of public or great general interest.The court found that neither exception applied to Petersen's dispute. It therefore concluded that there was no legal basis to continue examining his challenge to the calculation of the property proceeds.As a result, the court dismissed the appeal without deciding whether the trial court had correctly calculated Petersen's financial contributions or his share of the sale proceeds.You use AI every day. articles.title: Canadian family appeals for return of late mother's ashes after thieves steal urn in home break-in; police later find cremated remains at a funeral home with a note
articles.summary: A Canadian family appealed for the return of an urn containing a loved one’s ashes after it was stolen during a home break-in in Chestermere, Alberta.
articles.body: A Canadian family appealed for the return of an urn containing a loved one’s ashes after it was stolen during a home break-in in Chestermere, Alberta. According to Global News, Anna Thompson died at the age of 74 before Christmas, and her ashes were among the items taken from her son’s home on a Tuesday morning, days before her funeral on 17 January. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) made a compassionate appeal for their return and sought two male suspects. In an update dated 9 January 2026, the RCMP said the ashes had been safely returned to the family.What was stolen during the Canadian family’s home break-inAccording to the family, the house was broken into on a Tuesday morning. The outlet said the thieves entered through the backyard, forced open a back door and left with several items, including an iPad, money and tools. The family realised only later in the day that the ashes were also missing.The Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) said in a news release dated 8 January 2026 that officers responded on 6 January to a report of a break and enter at a residence in the Cove community of Chestermere. According to the RCMP, several personal items were stolen, including a case covered in red velvet that contained the ashes of a deceased loved one. The release said the loss had caused significant emotional distress to the family.What did the Canadian family ask the public to look forAccording to Global News, the family asked the public to watch for a red velvet bag containing a brown faux-leather box. The outlet reported that they also appealed directly to those responsible. "I have to have hope that they'll do the right thing," Deanna Thompson told Global News. She added that even an anonymous email indicating where the ashes could be found would help the family lay her mother to rest, and said the container includes identifying information and ways to return the remains.The RCMP described its own request as a compassionate appeal for the urn and ashes to be returned. The release stated that police believed the urn may have been taken unintentionally or discarded shortly after the break-in, and that its return was the priority because of the scheduled funeral. The release said anonymous tips could be given to Crime Stoppers.How were the stolen ashes returned to the Canadian familyThe RCMP release said police were also seeking help to identify two male suspects. It described the first as wearing white sweatpants, a blue and black coat, black shoes, and a black hat and gloves. The second was described as wearing blue overalls with yellow stripes and a white construction hat. Global News reported that the home has no security camera, but that video from a house across the street shows people the family believes may be connected to the break-in. The outlet said one individual in the footage appears to be dressed as a worker.In an update dated 9 January 2026, the RCMP said the cremated remains had been returned safely to the family. According to the update, they were left at a Calgary funeral home with a note asking for their safe return to the family. The RCMP said the investigation was continuing and that it was still seeking help to identify the two male suspects responsible for the break and enter and theft.You use AI every day. articles.title: Meet Leo Hartman, the 4-year-old who turned an imaginary doughnut shop into a real T-shirt business and raised $900
articles.summary: A four-year-old boy from Norman, Oklahoma, has turned an imaginary doughnut shop into a real fundraising initiative, raising $900 through T-shirt sales
articles.body: A four-year-old boy from Norman, Oklahoma, has turned an imaginary doughnut shop into a real fundraising initiative, raising $900 through T-shirt sales for a local animal shelter. Leo Hartman came up with the idea of ‘Old Western Town Donut Shop’, a pretend business that became popular after his father shared a video of it. Rather than keeping the money raised, Leo decided to donate the proceeds to Norman Animal Welfare, where his family had adopted their dog and several barn cats. His generosity did not stop there. After receiving a $400 award from First Fidelity Bank, he donated that money to the shelter too, taking his reported contribution to $1,300.How did Leo's imaginary doughnut shop become a real T-shirt businessLeo's idea began with an imaginary doughnut shop, which he created as part of his imaginative play. His father helped bring the concept to a wider audience by making a video featuring the pretend business. The family then turned the idea into a T-shirt-selling initiative, using the shop's name and concept for the merchandise.According to KFOR's report, the video helped sales take off, with the family receiving enough orders to raise $900. Although the doughnut shop existed only in Leo's imagination, the T-shirts became an actual product that people could purchase. The money raised through the sales was subsequently put towards a cause that was already important to the young boy and his family.Leo's family inspired his decision to support animal welfareLeo lives on a farm in Norman with his younger sister, Eliza, aged three, and his older brother, James, aged seven. The family has adopted their dog, Abby, and several barn cats from Norman Animal Welfare, making the organisation a familiar part of their lives. Leo decided that donating the money raised through his imaginary shop would be a way of thanking the shelter.KFOR reported that the family had a strong connection with animals, with all three children described as animal lovers. Leo's decision to donate the T-shirt profits meant that the money from his pretend business would support the organisation from which his family had adopted several pets. His initiative also attracted recognition from the shelter's management.Why did Leo donate his $400 Pay It 4Ward award to the shelterLeo's fundraising efforts received additional recognition when First Fidelity Bank presented him with a $400 Pay It 4Ward award. Rather than keeping the award money, he decided to give it to Norman Animal Welfare as well. Leo handed the money directly to Kellee Robertson, the shelter's manager.Robertson acknowledged the young boy's initiative and generosity, saying, “So young, and to come up with such a great idea!” She also added, “You know, it tells me that he’s going to grow up to be an amazing human being.” The additional award brought Leo's contribution to the shelter to $1,300, combining the $900 raised through T-shirt sales with the $400 recognition award.What celebration did the animal shelter organise in Leo's honourFollowing Leo's donation, Norman Animal Welfare, along with county and city staff, organised a celebration in his honour. The event included a doughnut party featuring real doughnuts, giving the young boy an opportunity to enjoy the treat behind his imaginary business concept. He also received a T-shirt and a hat, along with the opportunity to spend time with the animals at the shelter.The celebration also highlighted the potential benefit of his contribution for other animals awaiting adoption. Leo's donation would help support the shelter's animals, including those expected to use a dog park that was soon to be built at the facility. The park was intended to provide a place for the dogs to play while they waited to find homes.Why was Leo's family still accepting T-shirt ordersLeo's fundraising initiative did not end with the initial $900 in sales and the additional $400 award. At the time of KFOR's September 9, 2026, report, his family was still accepting orders for the imaginary doughnut shop T-shirts for one more week. The proceeds from these additional orders were also set to benefit Norman Animal Welfare. Leo's imaginary ‘Old Western Town Doughnut Shop’ had therefore become a real fundraising effort, with T-shirt sales and the bank's award contributing to a total donation of $1,300 reported by the news outlet.You use AI every day. articles.title: More than 2,000 donors raise £330,000 in 60 days to protect 340 acres around Dorset’s famous Cerne Abbas Giant, creating a new nature haven for rare butterflies
articles.summary: The Cerne Abbas Giant appeal reached its £330,000 target in 60 days, allowing the National Trust to buy 340 acres of Dorset countryside around Britain’s
articles.body: The Cerne Abbas Giant appeal reached its £330,000 target in 60 days, allowing the National Trust to buy 340 acres of Dorset countryside around Britain’s largest chalk hill figure. The charity, which has looked after the giant and a small plot of land around him since 1920, announced the result on 3 February 2026. More than 2,000 donors, including many Trust members, gave to the appeal, with gifts arriving from 20 countries. The land, which the charity says is equivalent in size to 190 football pitches, surrounds an iconic and mysterious monument that has captured people’s imaginations worldwide for generations.Cerne Abbas Giant appeal: how £330,000 was raised in 60 days from donors around the worldAccording to National Trust, the appeal launched in early December 2025 with backing from Sir Stephen Fry, and donations of every size arrived straight away, from £1 up to £32,000. Fry described the chance to protect such a large area of biodiverse countryside around the Giant as very rare.Gifts, grants and bequests worth more than £2 million had already kickstarted the project, so the appeal supplied the final piece needed for the purchase to go ahead. Sian Wilkinson, the Trust’s head of public fundraising, said in the announcement that every gift made the purchase possible. She said the Trust can now start creating a nature haven around the Giant, and that the appeal shows bold things can be done when people come together.National Trust plans a nature haven for rare butterflies around the Cerne Abbas Giant in DorsetHannah Jefferson, the Trust’s general manager for West Dorset and Cranborne Chase, said in the announcement that appeal donations, major donors, legacies, local businesses and grants all combined to make this once-in-a-lifetime purchase possible. The Trust now intends to create a patchwork of habitats that helps species adapt and thrive.Among the wildlife the project aims to support are 36 butterfly species, including the endangered Duke of Burgundy, which survives at just six sites in Dorset and is declining across the rest of England. The appeal page also names the Marsh Fritillary and the Adonis Blue among the rare butterflies living on Giant Hill. By joining up parcels of land around the hill, including a 59.5-hectare (147-acre) Site of Special Scientific Interest, the Trust will create 77 hectares (190 acres) of new habitat.Donors can see what their money does: the appeal page says £15 could create 36 square metres of wildflower grassland, giving the Duke of Burgundy shelter and food.Rangers, archaeologists and a re-chalking of the Giant: what happens next on the Dorset hillsideWork has begun to recruit a local area ranger, who will lead Trust staff, contractors and volunteers. The team also plans to work with organisations including Butterfly Conservation. Jefferson said the Trust will first get to know the site, talk to the community about its aspirations and local knowledge, and apply for further grants.The Giant was due to be re-chalked in early summer 2026 with help from 10 appeal donors, who won a place in a Crowdfunder prize draw. Together with staff and volunteers, they were to pack about 17 tonnes of chalk into its outline, which keeps weeds at bay and keeps it visible for miles around.The purchase also opens the way for archaeological research. A 2021 analysis found the Giant was probably first carved in the early medieval period, between the years 770 and 1100. Archaeologist Steve Timms said the acquisition allows research on a landscape scale, which will guide how the land is managed and help answer questions about settlement and ritual activity over several thousand years.The appeal itself remains open. The National Trust says on its appeal page that future donations will pay for habitat creation and wider access, shaped with local people. Its announcement adds that the money will help restore chalk grassland and plant trees.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: SC: Indians married here can't get divorced abroad
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Taking advantage of liberal laws abroad to obtain a divorce for a wedding solemnised in India will not automatically lead to dissolution of the
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Taking advantage of liberal laws abroad to obtain a divorce for a wedding solemnised in India will not automatically lead to dissolution of the marriage under Indian law, Supreme Court has ruled.Viewing negatively the use in a foreign court of grounds for divorce which are not recognised in India, SC said a person who contracts a second marriage on that basis may face prosecution for bigamy as the first marriage continues to subsist under Indian law, reports Amit Anand Choudhary.With many men approaching a foreign court to get a divorce on the ground of irretrievable breakdown of marriage - despite the wife opposing the plea - and thereafter remarrying, SC said the person has to face proceedings even in a case where he had become a citizen of a foreign country. The top court said legal consequences stemm-ing from the subsisting marriage cannot be overridden by a subsequent change in a spouse's nationality.Irretrievable breakdown of marriage no divorce ground in Indian law: SCThe bench of Justices Prashant Kumar Mishra and Shree Chandrashekhar allowed criminal proceedings for bigamy against a man who remarried after getting a divorce order from a foreign court on the ground of irretrievable breakdown of marriage in proceedings opposed by the wife. The court said that irretrievable breakdown of marriage is not a ground for divorce in Indian law and, therefore, the divorce granted by the foreign court is not valid.“In our view, the foreign divorce decree was passed in contravention of the existing matrimonial law in India and on a ground that is not even recognised statutorily. This violates the legal threshold of Section 13 of the CPC, which every foreign decree has to pass through,” the SC bench said.The bench also said that if the foreign decree does not satisfy the requirements of Section 13 of the Civil Procedure Code, then the husband, relying on such a decree, cannot be permitted to contend that his first marriage stood dissolved in the eyes of matrimonial laws of India and, thus, escape the rigours of Section 494 of IPC (marrying again during lifetime of husband or wife).“Now, coming to the argument of the husband that since he was a British citizen when the second marriage with second wife was solemnised and since the second marriage took place outside India, keeping in view the mandate of Section 4 of the IPC, he cannot be held liable. We cannot accept this submission in the manner canvassed as the husband was married to first wife in India under Hindu rites, rituals and customs; thus, even if the second marriage took place outside India, the allegations under Section 494 of the IPC cannot be said to be diluted since enquiry for the offence of bigamy cannot be confined to the place of second marriage but must necessarily take into account the subsisting matrimonial relationship...” the bench said.The court, however, quashed criminal proceedings against the parents and second wife of the man.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: A Texas estate said a 2009 deed carried its late owner's forged signature; after a man tied to the transfer was sentenced to 10 years, an appeals court ruled the estate could withdraw its claims against a later buyer
articles.summary: A disputed property deed can leave an estate fighting to recover land years after its owner's death, particularly when the signature authorising the
articles.body: A disputed property deed can leave an estate fighting to recover land years after its owner's death, particularly when the signature authorising the original transfer is alleged to be forged. In Texas, the estate of a deceased doctor challenged a 2009 property transfer, claiming that a man who controlled the company receiving the land had forged the owner's signature. The dispute later involved another company that purchased the property and sought to defend its ownership.In a November 6, 2026, memorandum opinion available on Justia, the Texas First Court of Appeals ruled that the estate could withdraw its claims against the later buyer, Malachite Venture Corporation. The court reversed the trial court's refusal to recognise the withdrawal and its subsequent decision granting summary judgment to the buyer on the estate's claims. The appeals court held that the estate had filed its notice of nonsuit before judgment was entered and that the withdrawal did not prevent the buyer from pursuing any independent claims for affirmative relief.How the disputed property transfer beganThe case concerned land originally conveyed to Shiva Investment Group in 1992. In 2009, a deed purported to transfer the property from Shiva Investment Group to The 2525 Brothers, L.P. The document carried the signature of Dr. R.K. Dhingra, who had signed on behalf of the investment group. However, Dhingra's estate later alleged that the signature was forged by David Scheffler, who controlled The 2525 Brothers. In 2010, the company transferred the property to Malachite Venture Corporation, making it the subsequent buyer in the disputed chain of ownership.After Dhingra died, his estate filed a lawsuit challenging the transaction and seeking to recover the property. It argued that because the 2009 deed was fraudulent, the subsequent transfer could not give Malachite valid ownership. The dispute also involved criminal proceedings against Scheffler. He was charged with securing the execution of documents by deception in connection with the disputed transaction. He was initially placed on deferred adjudication but was later adjudicated guilty and sentenced to 10 years in prison.Why the estate sought to withdraw its claimsDuring the property litigation, Shiva Investment Group executed a special warranty deed in 2018, transferring its interest in the property to Dhingra's estate. Malachite subsequently sought summary judgment against the estate. In its June 23, 2021, motion, the company argued that the estate could not maintain its title claims because neither Dhingra nor the estate owned the property when the original lawsuit was filed.Before the court could decide the summary judgment motion, however, the estate filed a notice of nonsuit, seeking to withdraw its claims against Malachite without prejudice. The withdrawal applied only to the estate's claims against the later buyer. It did not seek to dismiss the claims against Scheffler or the other defendants, nor did it attempt to eliminate any independent claims Malachite had filed.Malachite objected, arguing that the estate was attempting to avoid an unfavourable judgment after years of litigation. It also maintained that allowing the withdrawal would interfere with its ability to pursue its own counterclaims and cross-claims. The trial court accepted the objections, refused to recognise the nonsuit and subsequently granted summary judgment in Malachite's favour.Why the appeals court overturned the decisionThe estate challenged the trial court's decision, arguing that Texas law allowed it to withdraw its claims before a final judgment was entered. The appeals court examined Texas Rules of Civil Procedure 162 and 163. Rule 162 generally allows a plaintiff to take a nonsuit before introducing all its evidence at trial, except rebuttal evidence. The nonsuit becomes effective when the notice is filed and does not require judicial approval. Rule 163 also allows a plaintiff involved in a case with multiple defendants to dismiss its claims against one defendant, provided the withdrawal does not prejudice another party.The appeals court found that the estate had filed its notice before the trial court issued its summary judgment. Therefore, the withdrawal had already taken effect, and the lower court could no longer decide the merits of those particular claims. The judges also rejected the argument that the estate's decision to withdraw was automatically improper because it might have wanted to avoid an unfavourable ruling. A plaintiff's possible motivation does not, by itself, invalidate an otherwise permissible nonsuit.Why Malachite's objections were rejectedThe appeals court also considered whether withdrawing the estate's claims would unfairly harm Malachite. It explained that any counterclaims or cross-claims seeking independent affirmative relief would survive the nonsuit. The court noted that Malachite's pleadings were not included in the appellate record, but found that the withdrawal did not deprive the company of its right to pursue any such claims.The company could also pursue its interests in the remaining litigation involving Scheffler and the other defendants. The court found no sufficient evidence that the withdrawal increased Malachite's liability, removed a legal defence or deprived it of an opportunity to pursue its claims. Consequently, the requirements for allowing the nonsuit were satisfied, and the trial court had no adequate basis to refuse it.What happens nextIn its November 6, 2026, decision, the Texas First Court of Appeals reversed the orders refusing the estate's nonsuit and granting summary judgment to Malachite on the withdrawn claims. It remanded the case for further proceedings. The ruling does not determine whether the 2009 deed was forged or establish who ultimately owns the disputed property. It also does not eliminate any independent claims for affirmative relief that Malachite had properly pleaded against the estate or other parties.Overall, the decision clarifies that a plaintiff in Texas generally retains the right to withdraw its claims before judgment, even after years of litigation. A defendant's objection or concern about an unfavourable outcome does not automatically prevent that withdrawal, although any independent claims and available legal remedies can continue.You use AI every day. articles.summary: US President Donald Trump's envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff will meet Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Thursday, before travelling to
articles.body: US President Donald Trump's envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff will meet Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Thursday, before travelling to Ireland for talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Axios reported on Wednesday.The planned meetings come after two days of US-mediated talks between Russian and Ukrainian officials in Abu Dhabi, which ended with an agreement in principle on a major prisoner exchange.“One of the positives is we agreed that we're going to have the biggest humanitarian release of prisoners, which we're going to finalise the numbers tomorrow,” Kushner said after the talks.Russian delegation head Vladimir Medinsky and Ukraine's lead negotiator Rustem Umerov confirmed the planned exchange. The two countries have periodically exchanged prisoners during their nearly five-year war.The talks marked the first meeting between the Russian and Ukrainian delegations in nine months. However, expectations of a major breakthrough remained low, with Washington seeking to revive its peace efforts, which have so far failed to produce significant results.Zelenskyy described the proposed prisoner exchange as a positive development but maintained that Ukraine would not agree to demands to surrender territory occupied by Russia in exchange for peace.Meanwhile, fighting continued along the front lines, with both sides carrying out long-range missile and drone attacks. Three people were killed and 11 injured after a Russian daytime strike hit a market in the southern Odesa region, local authorities said. Residential buildings were also damaged, Oleh Kiper, head of the regional military administration, said.Overnight, Russian strikes on the Zaporizhzhia region and the eastern city of Kharkiv wounded seven civilians and damaged property, Ukrainian officials said.Russia's Defence Ministry said its forces had shot down 627 Ukrainian drones overnight, including 150 over the region surrounding St Petersburg. Regional Governor Alexander Drozdenko said the drones had sparked a fire at the port of Ust-Luga, a major Russian oil export facility, injuring three workers.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2020, a Texas woman planned a 160-square-foot backyard office but her HOA rejected it over height rules; in 2026, judges upheld $100,000 in legal fees after finding the restriction did not apply
articles.summary: In a Texas case, a homeowner challenged an association’s rejection of her proposed backyard office on the ground of an alleged height violation.
articles.body: In a Texas case, a homeowner challenged an association’s rejection of her proposed backyard office on the ground of an alleged height violation. Six years after the application was rejected, the Texas Third Court of Appeals awarded her $100,000 in attorney fees, leaving the homeowners’ association with the heavy legal tab.Backyard project faces oppositionThe dispute began in 2020 when Masha Davis, a resident of the Davis Spring subdivision in Williamson County, Texas, applied to build an accessory structure in her backyard. Davis described the proposed addition as a home office, while the homeowners’ association described it as a shed or shed-like structure in court proceedings.The Texas Third Court of Appeals said the association’s Architectural Review Committee denied the application, finding the proposed building exceeded the height allowed and rose above the roofline.Davis appealed, arguing that the recorded declaration of the community and its enforceable design guidelines did not include a height restriction that would prohibit her proposed structure. She sued Davis Spring Property Owners’ Association and its board president, Amanda Mock.Court finds no applicable height limitationThe issue in the case was the power of the association to enforce the architectural restrictions and whether the decision of the association was based upon the governing documents.The trial court considered the 2002 Design Guidelines, the only guidelines on record when Davis submitted her application. It concluded that those guidelines had no height limitation which prevented her accessory structure from being erected.Thus, the court concluded the architectural committee had no basis to deny the application on the stated height-related grounds. It also did not find any restrictive covenant that would prevent Davis from building the structure as submitted.The Texas Third Court of Appeals, in reviewing the later dispute over legal expenses, described these earlier findings.Long legal battle comes at steep priceDavis also made several other claims, including allegations involving breach of fiduciary duty and fair housing violations, which were dismissed during the proceedings, but Davis’s challenge to the restrictive covenants remained.The litigation was a legal marathon that lasted more than four years. Her lawyer submitted bills showing approximately 300 hours of attorney time and another 37 hours of paralegal time. The legal team asked for $149,680.25 in attorney fees, saying the work on the various claims was closely intertwined.The trial court eventually awarded Davis $100,000, a considerably smaller sum than he asked for. It also approved other contingent attorney fees for potential appeals and further proceedings.Appeals Court upholds award of $100,000The association and Mock appealed the fee award, asserting Davis could not recover legal expenses under Texas Property Code Section 5.006 and that her lawyer did not itemize costs related to different claims.The Texas Third Court of Appeals rejected both of those arguments, though. It said the association had not raised its objection to statutory entitlement in the original proceedings. The court also found that Davis’s attorney provided enough evidence to explain why the legal work was too intermingled to be meaningfully separated.The appellate court affirmed the trial court’s order on September 29, 2026, and the $100,000 award of attorney fees remained in place.The decision put another chapter to bed in a long-running neighborhood feud, and demonstrated how a HOA’s interpretation of its architectural guidelines can have huge financial consequences.Images Courtesy: Masha Devis and istockYou use AI every day. articles.title: Protesters clash with police, set fires  during Spain's general strike: Watch
articles.summary: Clashes broke out between masked protesters and police in Barcelona on Wednesday as tens of thousands of people took part in Spain's first general strike
articles.body: Clashes broke out between masked protesters and police in Barcelona on Wednesday as tens of thousands of people took part in Spain's first general strike in 14 years, called by the country's major trade unions over the housing affordability crisis and rising cost of living.Around 120,000 people joined demonstrations in Madrid and more than 50,000 gathered in Barcelona, where some protesters set fire to rubbish bins, smashed shop windows and clashed with police. Officers fired tear gas to disperse the crowds, while transport and other public services across the country faced significant disruption.The disturbances in Barcelona continued into the evening, with a heavy police presence in the city centre. Some clashes took place along Passeig de Gràcia, near the iconic Plaça de Catalunya. Local media reported that protesters fired fireworks at police and looted shops, including a Lego store. Some were also seen attempting to enter an Apple Store.The unions said around four million workers participated in the nationwide strike, which was backed by Spain's two largest labour organisations, the UGT and CCOO, as well as tenants' associations protesting against rising rents and evictions.UGT chief Pepe Álvarez described the strike as a success, citing "massive" participation, while CCOO leader Unai Sordo said turnout was "very significant". However, participation varied across the country, with stronger support in coastal regions where housing pressures have been particularly acute.The walkout was the first general strike in Spain since 2012, when workers protested against austerity measures during the eurozone debt crisis. It comes less than three weeks before parliamentary elections scheduled for November 29.Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez is seeking to make housing affordability a central election issue and shift the political debate away from corruption cases involving his inner circle and a deadly train crash last month. His Socialist Party, however, continues to trail in opinion polls.Spain faces a housing deficit of around 750,000 homes, which is projected to exceed one million by 2028, according to the country's central bank.With home ownership becoming increasingly unaffordable, demand for rental accommodation has risen sharply, putting further pressure on the market. The average monthly rent of 1,176 euros ($1,315) is equivalent to about 98.7 per cent of a young person's average monthly salary in Spain, according to the Youth Council of Spain.You use AI every day. articles.summary: A neglected alley in Hattiesburg, Mississippi, has been transformed into an unusual attraction filled with miniature artworks, a tiny movie theatre,
articles.body: A neglected alley in Hattiesburg, Mississippi, has been transformed into an unusual attraction filled with miniature artworks, a tiny movie theatre, colourful murals and a motion-activated dance spot. Known as the Hattiesburg Pocket Museum, the space offers visitors a closer look at small-scale creations displayed along an alley behind the Saenger Theater.A small creative project aimed at bringing life to an overlooked part of the city has grown into a popular local attraction. The Hattiesburg Convention Commission estimates more than 300,000 people have visited since 2020, as reported by The Associated Press. The attraction was created by Vicki and Rick Taylor, who turned the narrow passage into a place where art, miniature installations and unexpected details share space.How a small window display grew into a miniature art museumThe Hattiesburg Pocket Museum began as a small window display facing an alley behind the city's Saenger Theater. Vicki Taylor and her husband, Rick, opened it in 2020, during the COVID-19 shutdown. Their aim was to bring joy and more activity to downtown Hattiesburg at a time when businesses and public spaces were affected by the pandemic.The display grew into a collection of miniature scenes, with figurines positioned around electrical boxes, drainage pipes, and narrow corners. Some are easy to spot, while others are tucked into places that encourage visitors to look closely. The alley, once grey and smelly, gradually became a community hub and a destination for visitors.A tiny gallery, movie theatre and murals make the museum uniqueThe museum's displays extend beyond the original window. Visitors can find a tiny art gallery and a movie theatre, alongside colourful murals painted along the alley. Other features include a keychain and DVD exchange, as well as a rainbow bridge where people can leave collars belonging to pets that have died.A motion-activated dance spot adds another unexpected feature as it plays music and switches on disco lighting when someone approaches. Miniature figures are placed throughout the passage, including scenes of characters peering over electrical boxes and travelling down painted drainage pipes. The displays are often colourful and sometimes hidden, making careful observation part of the visit.How the museum is creating opportunities for local artistsVicki Taylor creates many of the miniature scenes in a cramped back room of the theatre. The Associated Press reported that she glues together tiny figurines and continues to curate exhibits that change over time. Taylor initially thought the attraction might lose momentum after the pandemic, but it continued to draw visitors.Her husband, Rick, is the executive director of the Hattiesburg Convention Commission, the organisation that runs both the museum and the theatre. The project has also given local artists a place to show their work. Gabby Smith, who painted several murals in the alley, said the experience helped build her confidence as she moved towards pursuing art as a full-time career.What makes Hattiesburg's miniature museum a popular visitor attractionThe Hattiesburg Convention Commission estimates that more than 300,000 people have visited the museum since it opened. Visit Hattiesburg CEO Marlo Dorsey linked the wider growth to efforts by city leaders to promote local culture, recreational activities and the arts.One initiative aims to paint 100 murals across the city. Dorsey also pointed to the Pocket Museum and the nearby Lucky Rabbit, a large vintage store known for its creative displays, as attractions that bring visitors to the area.You use AI every day. articles.title: Iran escalates in Hormuz, claims strike on Omani island it says 'enemy' uses for US military ops
articles.summary: Iran claims its Revolutionary Guard struck navigation equipment on Oman's Didamar Island in the Strait of Hormuz, but Omani officials dispute damage.
articles.body: Iran claims it struck a small Omani island in the Strait of Hormuz, targeting oil tanker navigation infrastructure as CENTCOM maintains its blockade of Iranian ports and protects commercial shipping from Iranian attacks along the southern route. Three sources also confirmed to Reuters Wednesday that navigation systems and communications equipment on Didamar Island, also known as Little Quoin Island, had been attacked, raising concerns about the vulnerability of maritime infrastructure used to maintain oil shipments through the Gulf. Iran's semiofficial Fars News Agency reported that the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) navy targeted the island, alleging the systems were being used to help vessels transit the strait without Tehran's authorization. WHITE HOUSE SILENT ON IRAN-OMAN HORMUZ PLAN TEHRAN SAYS WOULD BAN US WARSHIPS Iranian state television also claimed that personnel and equipment on the island "were helping the flow of oil smuggling by the enemy," with the IRGC maintaining it had carried out the strikes, Reuters reported. Video published by Reuters showed smoke rising near the rocky outcrop. The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said it identified the attack as occurring Nov. 8, before Iranian state media claimed responsibility on Nov. 10. ISW also questioned the extent of the reported damage, noting that commercial vessels continued using the southern route after the attack. "The extent of the damage to these systems and the systems struck remains unclear at the time of this writing," ISW said in its assessment. Satellite imagery from the European Union's Copernicus Sentinel-2 program, cited by Reuters and dated Nov. 8, also showed apparent scorch marks near radar and radio equipment on the island. TRADE VESSEL STRUCK BY PROJECTILE IN STRAIT OF HORMUZ AMID US-IRAN TALKS The strike comes as U.S. forces carry out missions to escort ships through the Strait of Hormuz, which connects the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea. The U.S. Navy imposed its blockade of Iranian ports in April after Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz in February amid escalating tensions. The U.S. lifted the blockade in June following a temporary ceasefire agreement, but then reinstated it in July. Commercial and allied shipping through the waterway is advised to use a southern route through Omani territorial waters, located outside of Tehran’s direct military control and overseen by CENTCOM. The latest incident on Didamar Island comes as Gulf oil exporters work to restore shipments disrupted by the conflict. TRUMP MEETS KEY IRAN WAR MEDIATOR AS UAE REVEALS MAJOR OIL EXPORT SURGE DESPITE CONFLICT According to Reuters, regional oil exports recovered to more than 80% of prewar levels in September and October, aided by CENTCOM and increased Saudi exports through the Red Sea. Shipping companies have also relied on offshore tanker-to-tanker transfers near Oman and the United Arab Emirates to maintain flows. Didamar, meanwhile, belongs to Oman, making the reported attack particularly sensitive as Tehran seeks to disrupt maritime operations in the region. It is a small, uninhabited rocky island roughly 10 nautical miles north of the tip of Oman's Musandam Peninsula, near one of the principal commercial shipping routes through the strait. The island has long served as a navigational landmark for vessels traveling along the waterway, including through a lighthouse established in 1914. Its maritime infrastructure reportedly includes a radar system mounted on a roughly 25-meter tower and radio communications equipment used to assist vessels navigating the narrow passage. The island has also been associated with the Hormuz Control Centre, which coordinates maritime traffic in the area. OIL SQUEEZE TIGHTENS AS IRAN-BACKED ATTACKS CRIPPLE HORMUZ ESCAPE ROUTES Arabian Maritime and Navigation Aids Services (AMMAS) has been identified as a provider of navigational support infrastructure in the region, including maritime lights, buoys and other equipment. The reported Didamar attack also follows U.S. military operations against Iranian targets elsewhere in the waterway. U.S. forces struck targets on Iran's Qeshm Island Nov. 2, and officials described the strikes as "defensive" actions targeting Iranian surface-to-air missile threats. Qeshm Island, located near the Strait of Hormuz, is home to Iranian naval facilities and military infrastructure associated with the Revolutionary Guard. President Donald Trump also acknowledged Nov. 6 that American forces continue to conduct limited strikes against Iranian targets. articles.title: A Washington nephew lived rent-free for 14 years in a house owned by his aunt and uncle, then claimed ownership after his aunt died; a November 9 appeals court upheld the uncle's right to remove him
articles.summary: Living in a family-owned home for years without paying rent does not necessarily give someone the right to claim ownership of the property.
articles.body: Living in a family-owned home for years without paying rent does not necessarily give someone the right to claim ownership of the property. A Washington man who spent 14 years living in a house belonging to his aunt and uncle discovered this after his aunt died and her husband sought to remove him from the property. Although the nephew had maintained the house, carried out improvements and occasionally paid utility bills, he argued that his long occupation had given him ownership rights.In an unpublished opinion dated November 9, 2026, the Washington Court of Appeals, Division One, upheld a lower court's decision in favour of the uncle, Jack Lyons. The ruling in Jack Lyons v. Curtis Reep, available on Justia, rejected Curtis Reep's claim of adverse possession and affirmed the order granting Lyons ownership of the property and a writ of ejectment. The court concluded that Reep had not provided sufficient evidence that the original permission to live there had been withdrawn by both owners, a crucial requirement for his ownership claim.Nephew lived in the property for 14 years without paying rentThe dispute concerned a single-family house on a residential lot in Tukwila, Washington. Jack Lyons and his wife, Leota Lyons, purchased the property in November 2001. It became part of their marital community property, meaning both spouses held an interest in it. In 2011, Leota's nephew, Curtis Reep, moved into the house. He continued living there until 2025, a period of approximately 14 years. During this time, he did not sign a rental agreement or pay rent to either of the owners.Reep also took responsibility for several maintenance and improvement activities. Between 2012 and 2015, he arranged or carried out painting, landscaping, yard work, tree maintenance, cleaning and house repairs. He also graded part of the property and installed a paved parking path. At different times, he made payments towards the property's water and electricity bills. However, the arrangement eventually became a source of disagreement. Between 2013 and 2015, Jack expressed his desire for Reep to leave and objected to the nephew's grading and paving work.In January 2025, Leota died. Five months later, her estate's personal representative transferred her interest in the property to Jack, in accordance with her will. Jack subsequently asked Reep to vacate the house, but he refused.Uncle approached the court to recover the houseIn August 2025, Jack filed a lawsuit in King County Superior Court, seeking to establish his ownership of the property and obtain an order allowing Reep's removal. Reep represented himself in the proceedings and filed a counterclaim based on adverse possession. He argued that although he had initially been allowed to live in the house, his occupation eventually became hostile to the owners' interests.Under Washington law, adverse possession allows someone to acquire ownership of land under specific circumstances, even without holding its legal title. However, the claimant must establish that possession was open and notorious, actual and uninterrupted, exclusive and hostile to the legal owner's interests. These conditions must exist together for at least 10 years under Washington's 10-year statute of limitations for recovering real property, RCW 4.16.020.The lower court granted Jack's request for summary judgment, concluding that Reep had not established the necessary conditions for adverse possession. It also ordered that title be confirmed in Jack's favour and authorised a writ of ejectment, allowing the nephew to be removed from the property. Reep appealed the decision.Appeals court found no evidence that both owners withdrew permissionThe appeals court focused on whether Reep's initially permitted occupation had subsequently become hostile to the owners' interests. It explained that permission to occupy a property generally prevents that occupation from qualifying as hostile possession. This is particularly important when someone initially enters a property with the owner's consent.The judges also considered that the house was marital community property. Under Washington law, one spouse cannot give away community property without the express or implied consent of the other spouse. The court applied the same reasoning to permission to occupy the property and its subsequent withdrawal. The evidence showed that both Jack and Leota had allowed Reep to live there in 2011. Jack's declaration stated that he had permitted his nephew to move into the house, while Reep himself said Leota had told him she was gifting the property to him.Although Jack had expressed objections and asked Reep to find somewhere else to live, the appeals court found no admissible evidence establishing that Leota had also withdrawn her permission. It therefore concluded that Reep had not demonstrated that the marital community's permission had been effectively revoked.Property improvements did not make the occupation hostileReep also argued that his improvements, particularly the construction of a paved parking area, demonstrated that he was treating the property as his own. However, the appeals court disagreed. It found that the work was consistent with the permission he had received to occupy a residential property. Maintaining the house, landscaping the grounds and installing a parking area did not, by themselves, establish hostile possession. The court ultimately found no genuine dispute over a material fact that would require a trial. It affirmed the lower court's summary judgment, the decision confirming Jack's title and the writ of ejectment.Overall, the ruling clarifies that living in a relative's property for many years, maintaining it and making improvements do not automatically establish ownership through adverse possession. When occupation begins with permission, a claimant must also provide sufficient evidence that the permission was effectively withdrawn and that all the legal requirements for adverse possession were subsequently met. In this case, Reep failed to establish that requirement, allowing his uncle to retain ownership and pursue his removal from the house.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Democrat Scott Colom becomes Mississippi's first Black senator since 1874
articles.summary: Democrat Scott Colom has defeated Republican incumbent Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi's closely contested US Senate race, becoming the state's
articles.body: Democrat Scott Colom has defeated Republican incumbent Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi's closely contested US Senate race, becoming the state's first Black senator since the Reconstruction era following the US Civil War.Colom, a 43-year-old district attorney, secured the narrow victory after several days of ballot counting in one of the last outstanding races from November 3 midterm elections. US media projected his victory this Wednesday.The result marks a significant political shift in Mississippi, a state that has long been dominated by white conservatives. It also adds to the Democrats' gains in the midterm elections, in which the party won control of both chambers of Congress.Hyde-Smith, 67, who was first elected in 2018, had consistently led in opinion polls in a state that President Donald Trump won by nearly 23 percentage points in 2024. Trump also campaigned for her towards the end of the race.Colom capitalised on Mississippi's large Black population, economic discontent and criticism of Hyde-Smith's record as the Republican sought a second full term. He also focused on grassroots campaigning, reaching voters through town halls, visits to public housing, festivals and food trucks."We did it the hard way, the grassroots way," Colom said.In an October interview with Reuters, he said Mississippi voters felt "betrayed" by Trump's policies, including the war in Iran, which has driven up fuel prices.During the campaign, Colom also stressed the need for a political party that could represent voters across racial and geographic divides."They actually deserve a senator that will listen to them, that actually cares about what they think, actually cares about what they're going through," he said."It's got to be about having a party that represents rural America again, suburban America, urban America — a party that makes sure we actually deliver for voters in ways that make their lives better, and we don't come up with excuses as to why we can't do it," he added.The last time Mississippi elected a Democrat to the Senate was in 1982, when John Stennis won the seat. The last Black candidate elected to the Senate from the state was former slave Blanche Bruce in 1874.In 2023, Hyde-Smith blocked Colom's nomination by former President Joe Biden to serve as a federal district judge in northern Mississippi, citing his position on transgender issues. Mississippi's other Republican senator, Roger Wicker, had supported his nomination.Colom's campaign also had received a boost from October rallies featuring Democratic Senators Raphael Warnock of Georgia and Cory Booker of New Jersey.You use AI every day.
